title: Why people trust or distrust institutions

lines.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at a question that sits at the centre of public administration: why do people trust some institutions and distrust others?
Researchers usually begin by separating two ideas that are often confused.
Trust is a belief about what an institution will do, while trustworthiness is a fact about whether it deserves that belief. The two do not always match.
A hospital can be excellent and still distrusted, and a careless agency can be trusted for years.
The first explanation is performance. People judge institutions by what they deliver: clean water, punctual trains, a pension that arrives on time.
Studies in several countries show that when services improve, trust rises, but slowly. The reverse is quicker.
A single visible failure, such as a bridge collapse, can erase years of gradual gains.
Psychologists call this negativity bias, and it explains why bad news travels so much further than good news.
The second explanation concerns process rather than results. Procedural fairness means that people accept an unwelcome decision if they believe it was reached honestly.
In one well-known type of experiment, participants who lost a dispute were more satisfied if they had explained their side than if they had won unheard.
So being listened to matters at least as much as the outcome.
The third explanation is transparency, and here the picture is more complicated than most reformers expect. It seems obvious that publishing information should increase trust. Often it does.
But when an institution publishes data that reveal mistakes, trust can fall in the short term.
The advantage appears later, because people begin to believe that problems will be found and corrected rather than hidden.
So transparency is a long-term investment, not a quick repair.
A fourth factor is closeness. People tend to trust local institutions more than national ones, partly because they can see the people who work there.
A town clerk is a neighbour; a ministry is an abstraction. Personal contact is usually, though not always, positive.
Finally, we must consider history and culture. In societies where public officials have long taken bribes, citizens learn to expect corruption and behave accordingly.
They pay, because everyone pays. That behaviour then confirms the expectation, and a cycle forms. Breaking it is difficult, because trust cannot be ordered by law.
Reformers who succeed tend to do three things. They start with one visible service and fix it completely. They punish a few high-profile offenders fairly and openly.
And they keep going for years, as one campaign is never enough.
To summarise, trust is built slowly through performance, fairness, openness and personal contact, and it is lost quickly.
For your assignment, choose one institution you know well and explain which of these factors is the most important in its case.
Please submit it in two weeks, and keep it under one thousand five hundred words.

title: Bias in human and machine decisions

lines.t: Welcome back. Last week we asked whether machines can be fair.
This week I want to put that question next to an uncomfortable fact: human decision makers are not especially fair either. Any honest comparison has to start there.
Let me begin with people. Decades of research show that human judgement is affected by things that have nothing to do with the case.
A well-known study of parole hearings reported that decisions varied with the time since the judges' last break.
I should say that later researchers argued the pattern might partly come from the order in which cases were scheduled, so we should treat the original claim cautiously.
Even so, the broader finding is solid: the same person can reach different conclusions about identical cases on different days.
Psychologists call this noise, and distinguish it from bias. Bias is a consistent push in one direction. Noise is random scatter.
A scale that always reads two kilos too heavy is biased; a scale that gives a different number each time is noisy. Human systems suffer from both.
Now to machines. A common first reaction is that an algorithm is neutral because it has no feelings. That is mistaken.
A model learns from historical data, and if the data record past discrimination, the model can reproduce it.
A famous kind of example involves hiring tools trained on the résumés of previous successful employees.
If most of those employees were men, the system may learn to prefer features that correlate with being male, even when gender is never mentioned.
This is called proxy discrimination.
However, machines have one real advantage: consistency. Given the same input, a model returns the same output every time. So it removes noise, even if it keeps bias.
Furthermore, a model can be audited. We can test it with thousands of artificial cases, change one detail at a time, and see whether the result changes.
We cannot do this with a human judge, who will remember the experiment and may change behaviour.
There is a catch, though. Researchers have shown that there are several mathematical definitions of fairness, and in most real situations they cannot all be satisfied at once.
For example, you can demand that the error rate is the same for two groups, or that a given score means the same risk for both groups.
If the groups differ in the underlying rate of the event, you cannot have both. This does not mean that fairness is impossible.
It means that someone must choose which definition matters, and that choice is a moral and legal one, not a technical one.
So what is the practical conclusion? Most experts now favour what is called human oversight, but we have to be careful with that phrase.
Studies suggest that people supervising a system often follow its recommendation even when it is wrong, a habit known as automation bias.
Oversight works only if the human has time, training and the genuine power to disagree.
In short: people are noisy and biased, machines are consistent and biased, and the sensible question is not which is perfect but which can be examined, challenged and improved.
For next week, read the two articles on the course page, and think about which definition of fairness you would choose for a court.

lines.t: Good morning. Today's topic sounds simple: how do we measure corruption? The difficulty is obvious.
People who pay or accept bribes do not report them, so there is no direct count.
Researchers have therefore developed several indirect methods, and each has strengths and weaknesses.
The first and most famous approach is the perception index. These indices combine surveys of business people and country experts to produce a score.
They are popular because they cover almost every country and can be compared across years. But they measure what people think, not what happens.
And perceptions can lag behind reality: a country may clean up its customs service, yet continue to be seen as corrupt for years.
The second approach is experience surveys. Instead of asking what people believe, interviewers ask households whether they paid a bribe to any official during the previous twelve months.
This is closer to real behaviour. The weakness is honesty: people may be ashamed or afraid to answer, so the numbers are probably too low.
To reduce this problem, some researchers use a technique called a list experiment.
Half of the respondents see a list of four harmless activities and say how many they did.
The other half see the same list plus a fifth item, paying a bribe.
The difference in averages between the groups estimates the share of bribe payers, though nobody has to admit to anything.
A third family of methods uses hard data. Take public procurement.
Analysts can examine contracts and look for warning signs: only one bidder, a very short advertising period, or frequent changes to the price after signing.
None of these proves a crime, but a pattern of red flags points investigators to where they should look.
The huge advantage is that the data already exist and can be analysed every day. The disadvantage is that corrupt officials learn which signs are watched and adapt.
The fourth approach is more creative. Economists have estimated corruption by measuring leakage.
For example, if a government budget says that one hundred schools should receive textbooks, researchers visit the schools to check what arrived.
The gap between the budget and the delivery is the loss.
This is a good method for specific programmes, but it cannot show how much of the loss is theft and how much is simple waste or poor record keeping.
Finally, some studies use natural experiments. When auditors visit a randomly chosen municipality, the amount of misused money they find can be compared with that in similar places.
Such studies show that audits do reduce misuse in the places they visit, and sometimes in neighbouring places too.
What should we conclude? No single measure is reliable on its own.
The best practice is to combine them, so that the weaknesses of one are covered by the strengths of another.
And whichever indicator you use, always ask what exactly it measures. Is it perception, experience or a statistical sign?
For the next session, please bring an example of an indicator from a report you have read, and be ready to explain which of these approaches it belongs to.

title: The psychology of persuasion in the courtroom

lines.t: Good evening.
Tonight we look at a question that lawyers have asked for centuries, and psychologists for about a hundred years: what makes a jury believe one story rather than another?
Let me start with a common belief, which is that jurors weigh up each piece of evidence like accountants adding up numbers. Research suggests otherwise.
Most jurors build a story. They take the facts they hear and arrange them into an account of what happened, with a beginning, a motive and an ending.
The story that is most complete and consistent tends to win, even if some of its details are weaker than those in the competing version.
Second, order matters. Experiments with mock juries find a primacy effect: information heard first leaves a strong impression.
Yet there is also a recency effect, since the last thing heard is easiest to remember. Which dominates depends on the length of the trial.
In short trials, the final speech has more influence.
In long trials, where jurors hear weeks of evidence, the opening statement tends to shape how everything afterwards is understood.
So experienced lawyers use their openings to give jurors a frame.
Third, the way witnesses speak. Many people assume that a confident witness is an accurate one.
In fact, studies of eyewitnesses show only a weak connection between confidence and accuracy, particularly when the confidence is expressed long after the event.
Nevertheless, jurors are strongly influenced by confidence.
A witness who hesitates and says, I think, perhaps, may be completely right and still be believed less than one who speaks firmly and is wrong.
Fourth, the effect of expert witnesses. Jurors usually treat a scientist as especially credible, but credibility is not the same as clarity.
An expert who uses technical language may seem impressive at first yet be less persuasive than one who explains a result with an everyday comparison.
In several experiments, an expert who used a simple analogy produced greater understanding and also greater agreement.
Fifth, emotion. Photographs of injuries, for example, can make jurors angrier at the defendant.
Courts know this, so judges are expected to weigh how much a picture proves against how much it might inflame.
Interestingly, studies suggest that instructions to disregard something a juror has already heard often fail.
In some cases they make the information more memorable, a result known as the backfire effect, although the evidence for this is mixed.
What does this mean for justice? Not that persuasion is a trick. Clear stories, fair order and honest explanation help jurors understand a case.
The danger lies in techniques that exploit weaknesses rather than helping understanding. That is why many legal systems regulate what lawyers may say in closing arguments.
For the assignment, take a famous trial from any country, read the summary, and identify which of the five influences we discussed was most visible.
You have until the fifteenth of next month.

title: How the brain consolidates memory during sleep

lines.t: Good morning. Most students believe that sleep is time off for the brain, a period when nothing useful happens.
Today I want to show you that the reverse is closer to the truth: sleep is when much of what you learned during the day is stored.
The key idea is memory consolidation, the process by which a fragile new memory becomes stable and long lasting.
When you learn something, a region deep in the brain called the hippocampus records it quickly. You can think of the hippocampus as a temporary notebook.
It writes fast but has limited space. The cortex, the outer layer of the brain, is more like a library.
It stores information for decades, but it learns slowly. Consolidation is the transfer of information from the notebook to the library, and it happens mainly while you sleep.
Sleep is not a single state. It has stages, and they appear in cycles of about ninety minutes.
Early in the night, most of the time is spent in deep sleep, sometimes called slow wave sleep because the brain's electrical activity forms long, slow waves.
Later in the night, rapid eye movement sleep, or REM, becomes longer. Researchers believe the stages play different roles.
Deep sleep seems especially important for facts and events, what psychologists call declarative memory.
During slow waves, the hippocampus replays the pattern of activity it showed during learning, in a compressed form, and sends it to the cortex.
Short bursts of fast activity, called sleep spindles, appear at the same time and seem to help with the transfer.
In one classic design, volunteers learned pairs of words in the evening.
Those who slept remembered considerably more pairs the next morning than those who stayed awake for the same period.
REM sleep, by contrast, seems to be more important for emotional memories and for skills. It may also help the brain to combine information in new ways.
Volunteers who were given a puzzle with a hidden shortcut were more likely to discover it after a night's sleep than after the same time awake.
I should mention that these studies involve small groups, and scientists are still debating how strongly each stage is tied to each type of memory.
What does this mean in practice? First, an all-night revision session before an exam may be counterproductive.
You may gain a few extra hours of study, but you lose the processing that makes the information stable.
Second, a short nap of around twenty minutes can improve alertness, while a longer nap of ninety minutes can include a full cycle and help consolidation.
Third, studying difficult material shortly before bedtime might give the brain more to work on.
The evidence for this is weaker, so I would not rely on it alone.
Finally, a word of caution. Sleep does not replace practice. Consolidation strengthens what you have already learned; it does not create knowledge from nothing.
So the formula for good learning is simple: study with attention, sleep well, and review the next day.
For the next lecture, please keep a sleep diary for one week and note your study times. We will use them as a class data set.
